Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use breast-cancer.csv, which contains 569 cases from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Predict y (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using mean_radius, mean_texture, and mean_smoothness.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{5,15,25,35,45}. k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.

Using the estimated probabilities for y = 1 on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

I use the supplied 70/30 split in data/breast-cancer-split.csv (398 training, 171 test), so there is no random component and no seed is needed.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

data = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")
split = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer-split.csv")
assert (split["row"].to_numpy() == np.arange(1, len(data) + 1)).all()   # rows match by position

features = ["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]
is_train = (split["split"] == "train").to_numpy()
X, y = data[features].to_numpy(), data["y"].to_numpy()

mean, sd = X[is_train].mean(axis=0), X[is_train].std(axis=0, ddof=0)   # training statistics only
X_train, X_test = (X[is_train] - mean) / sd, (X[~is_train] - mean) / sd
y_train, y_test = y[is_train], y[~is_train]

models = {"Logistic": LogisticRegression(penalty=None, max_iter=10000)}
for k in [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]:
    models[f"KNN k={k}"] = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform", algorithm="brute")

styles = ["-", "--", "--", "--", "--", "--"]
plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 5))
auc_rows = []
for (name, model), ls in zip(models.items(), styles):
    p_test = model.fit(X_train, y_train).predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, p_test)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test)
    auc_rows.append((name, auc))
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, ls, lw=2 if name == "Logistic" else 1.3, label=f"{name} (AUC {auc:.3f})")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", lw=0.7, linestyle=":")
plt.xlabel("False positive rate"); plt.ylabel("True positive rate")
plt.title("Test ROC curves"); plt.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

pd.DataFrame(auc_rows, columns=["model", "test AUC"]).round(4)
model test AUC
0 Logistic 0.9746
1 KNN k=5 0.9329
2 KNN k=15 0.9480
3 KNN k=25 0.9599
4 KNN k=35 0.9727
5 KNN k=45 0.9741

I prefer logistic regression: it has the highest test AUC (0.9750.975), though KNN with k=45k=45 is essentially tied (0.9740.974). KNN improves steadily with kk (from 0.9330.933 at k=5k=5), since larger neighborhoods smooth the noisy probability estimates. Given the near-tie on 171 test cases, logistic regression wins on simplicity: no tuning parameter and interpretable coefficients.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{1,3,5,10,20}. k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its kk nearest neighbors.

For each kk, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with kk. In particular, explain what happens at k=1k=1 and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Same split and standardization as Question 1.

ks = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 3.4), sharey=True)
rows = []
for ax, k in zip(axes, ks):
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform", algorithm="brute").fit(X_train, y_train)
    # predicting on the training data keeps each observation among its own k neighbors
    for label, Xs, ys, color in [("train", X_train, y_train, "C0"), ("test", X_test, y_test, "C1")]:
        p = knn.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1]
        fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(ys, p)
        auc = roc_auc_score(ys, p)
        rows.append((k, label, auc))
        ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=color, label=f"{label} (AUC {auc:.3f})")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", lw=0.7, linestyle=":")
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}"); ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate"); ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["k", "set", "AUC"]).pivot(index="k", columns="set", values="AUC")[["train", "test"]].round(4)
set train test
k
1 1.0000 0.8764
3 0.9905 0.9138
5 0.9847 0.9329
10 0.9862 0.9446
20 0.9880 0.9586

Training AUC is higher than test AUC for every kk, and the gap shrinks as kk grows (from 1.0001.000 vs. 0.8760.876 at k=1k=1 to 0.9880.988 vs. 0.9590.959 at k=20k=20). At k=1k=1 each training point’s single nearest neighbor is itself, so its predicted probability is exactly its own label and the training ROC is perfect regardless of how well the model generalizes. Larger kk dilutes the self-match, so the training fit becomes less optimistic. Training performance does not reflect new observations because the model has already seen the training labels; only the test curve measures performance on unseen cases.

Selected item: [classmate’s report/repository] — Homework 5, Question 1, part (b).

1. Mistake. The write-up says the KNN variance approaches σ2/k\sigma^2/k, but its own table shows the variance staying far above σ2/k\sigma^2/k for every kk.

2. Assessment. The report states: “variance falls from 0.037 at k = 1 toward σ²/k as more responses are averaged.” With σ=0.1\sigma=0.1, σ2/k=0.01/k\sigma^2/k=0.01/k, which is 0.0100.010 at k=1k=1 and 0.00030.0003 at k=29k=29. The report’s simulated variance is 0.0370.037 and 0.00750.0075 at those values: 3.73.7 times and about 2222 times larger. Variance falls from k=1k=1 to k=9k=9 and then declines only slowly (0.00950.0095 at k=9k=9 vs. 0.00750.0075 at k=29k=29), unlike the 1/k1/k decay the sentence implies. The reason is that σ2/k\sigma^2/k is only the noise variance when the neighbor locations are held fixed. In this simulation each repetition also draws new training covariates, so the selected neighbors change, and so does the average of ff over them. That second source dominates the variance. By the law of total variance, Var⁡(f̂k(𝒙0))=σ2k⏟noise given neighbors+Var⁡(1k∑i∈Nkf(𝑿i))⏟changing neighborhoods. \operatorname{Var}(\hat f_k(\mathbf x_0)) =\underbrace{\tfrac{\sigma^2}{k}}_{\text{noise given neighbors}} +\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\tfrac1k\textstyle\sum_{i\in N_k}f(\mathbf X_i)\Big)}_{\text{changing neighborhoods}} .

3. Correction. The verification below repeats the experiment (seed 60501) and separates the two components.

rng = np.random.default_rng(60501)
f = lambda X: 0.5 * X[:, 0] + np.sin(X[:, 1]) - 0.3 * X[:, 2] ** 2
x0 = np.array([0.5, 0.7, 1.0])
ks, n, nsim, sigma = np.arange(1, 30, 2), 400, 200, 0.1

pred = np.zeros((nsim, len(ks)))      # usual KNN estimate
pred_f = np.zeros((nsim, len(ks)))    # average of f over the same neighbors (no response noise)
for r in range(nsim):
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, 3))
    y = f(X) + rng.normal(0, sigma, n)
    order = np.argsort(((X - x0) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    pred[r] = (np.cumsum(y[order]) / np.arange(1, n + 1))[ks - 1]
    pred_f[r] = (np.cumsum(f(X)[order]) / np.arange(1, n + 1))[ks - 1]

total = pred.var(axis=0)                    # divisor 200
neighborhood = pred_f.var(axis=0)
noise = sigma ** 2 / ks
print(pd.DataFrame({"k": ks, "variance": total, "sigma^2/k": noise,
                    "neighborhood part": neighborhood,
                    "sum of parts": noise + neighborhood}).round(5).iloc[::2].to_string(index=False))

plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
plt.plot(ks, total, "o-", label="Simulated variance")
plt.plot(ks, noise, "s--", label=r"$\sigma^2/k$ (noise part only)")
plt.plot(ks, neighborhood, "^:", label="Changing-neighborhood part")
plt.xlabel("Number of neighbors k"); plt.ylabel("Variance at $x_0$"); plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
 k  variance  sigma^2/k  neighborhood part  sum of parts
 1   0.03934    0.01000            0.02928       0.03928
 5   0.01410    0.00200            0.01165       0.01365
 9   0.00971    0.00111            0.00831       0.00942
13   0.00778    0.00077            0.00732       0.00809
17   0.00769    0.00059            0.00716       0.00775
21   0.00687    0.00048            0.00644       0.00692
25   0.00691    0.00040            0.00660       0.00700
29   0.00653    0.00034            0.00630       0.00664

The simulated variance equals the sum of the two parts up to Monte Carlo error, and it is 44 to 1919 times σ2/k\sigma^2/k across the grid. The corrected sentence for the report: “Variance falls from about 0.04 at k=1k=1 to about 0.007 at k=29k=29, but it remains far above σ2/k\sigma^2/k, because it also reflects how the selected neighbors change from one training set to the next, not only the response noise.” Adding a σ2/k\sigma^2/k reference curve to Figure 1 would make this visible.
